correction: Each of the students has submitted the assignment on time.
explanation: 'Each' is singular, so the verb must be 'has submitted'.

correction: She is an honest and hard-working employee.
explanation: 'Honest' starts with a vowel sound (silent h), so it needs 'an'.

correction: We have been living in this city for five years and we love it.
explanation: Use 'for' with a length of time; 'since' needs a starting point.

correction: Yesterday I went to the market with my mother to buy vegetables.
explanation: 'Yesterday' needs the simple past: went.

correction: My friend and I went to the cinema after finishing our exams.
explanation: This is the subject of the sentence, so use 'I', not 'me'.

correction: The quality of these mangoes is not very good.
explanation: The subject is 'the quality', which is singular, so use 'is'.

correction: This is the tallest building in our city.
explanation: Do not use 'most' with an -est superlative; just say 'the tallest'.

correction: I have been working in this company since 2019, and I enjoy it.
explanation: An action that started in the past and continues now, with 'since', needs the present perfect continuous.

correction: He is married to a doctor who works at the city hospital.
explanation: We are married 'to' someone.

correction: You should make a decision before the end of the day.
explanation: We 'make' a decision; 'do a decision' is not used.

correction: You must complete the form before Monday.
explanation: Modal verbs like 'must' are followed by the base verb without 'to'.

correction: Although he was tired, he continued working on the report.
explanation: Use either 'although' or 'but', never both in the same sentence.
The sentence is correct: the present perfect continuous with 'for two years' describes an ongoing habit.

correction: The sun rises in the east and sets in the west.
explanation: Compass directions as places take 'the': in the east, in the west.

correction: Neither the teacher nor the students were ready for the surprise test.
explanation: With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'the students' (plural).

correction: The committee has announced its decision after a long meeting.
explanation: 'Its' is the possessive; 'it's' means 'it is'.

correction: If I had known about the meeting, I would have attended it.
explanation: The if-part of a third conditional uses the past perfect: if I had known.

correction: Can you tell me where the nearest post office is?
explanation: In an indirect question the word order is subject + verb: where the post office is.

correction: The number of accidents on this road has increased sharply this year.
explanation: 'The number of' is singular, so it takes 'has increased'.

correction: The manager explained to us the new rules in detail.
explanation: We explain something 'to' someone; 'explain us' is incorrect.
The sentence is correct: an action in progress (were playing) interrupted by another (started).

correction: She doesn't like spicy food, so she ordered a plain dosa.
explanation: With 'she', the negative is 'doesn't', not 'don't'.

correction: My brother is older than me by three years.
explanation: 'Older' is already a comparative; do not add 'more'.

correction: He is very good at solving maths problems.
explanation: The fixed phrase is 'good at' something.

correction: You should not worry about the result too much.
explanation: 'Should' is followed by the base verb: should not worry.
The sentence is correct: 'despite' is followed by a noun phrase (the heavy rain).

correction: By the time the guests arrived, we had already finished cooking.
explanation: Something completed before another past event needs the past perfect: had finished.

correction: I am looking forward to meeting you at the conference next week.
explanation: In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by the -ing form.

correction: No sooner did he reach the station than the train left.
explanation: 'No sooner' is always paired with 'than', not 'when'.

correction: Bread and butter is my favourite breakfast.
explanation: 'Bread and butter' is a single dish, so it takes a singular verb.

correction: We will meet on Monday at 10 a.m. near the library.
explanation: Use 'at' with clock times.
The sentence is correct: after 'before' we use the present tense for a future action.

correction: When I reached the cinema, the film had already started, so we missed the beginning.
explanation: The film started before I arrived, so use the past perfect: had already started.

correction: One of my cousins lives in Bengaluru and works at a bank.
explanation: The subject is 'one', which is singular, so use 'lives'.

correction: She has never been late for work in her life.
explanation: 'Never' is already used; repeating it at the end is wrong.

correction: You needn't bring any food, we have plenty.
explanation: As a modal, 'needn't' is followed by the base verb without 'to'.

correction: Hardly had I closed my eyes when I heard a loud noise.
explanation: 'Hardly' is paired with 'when', not 'than'.
The sentence is correct: 'Had I known' is an inverted form of 'If I had known' (third conditional).

correction: Of all the students in the class, Meena is the most hardworking.
explanation: Comparing one person with a whole group needs the superlative: the most hardworking.

correction: The list of items is on the table.
explanation: The subject is 'the list', which is singular, so use 'is'.

correction: He prefers tea to coffee in the morning.
explanation: We prefer one thing 'to' another, not 'than'.

correction: The company has made a lot of progress in the last year.
explanation: A period of time takes 'in': in the last year.

correction: I want to buy a useful book on public speaking for my exam.
explanation: 'Useful' starts with a 'yoo' sound (a consonant sound), so it takes 'a'.
The sentence is correct: the present continuous describes a current course of study.

correction: Who do you think will win the singing competition this year?
explanation: The pronoun is the subject of 'will win', so use 'who', not 'whom'.

correction: Unless you practise regularly, you will not improve.
explanation: 'Unless' already means 'if not', so do not add another 'not'.

correction: The principal gave us a lot of advice before the exam.
explanation: 'Advice' is uncountable: a lot of advice, some advice, a piece of advice.
The sentence is correct: with 'neither ... nor' the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'the teacher' (singular).

correction: Last week we visited the science museum with our teachers.
explanation: 'Last week' needs the simple past: visited.

correction: Could you lend me your notes for a day?
explanation: You 'lend' something to someone; you 'borrow' something from someone.

correction: Rarely do we get such a good opportunity to travel abroad.
explanation: After a negative adverb like 'rarely' at the start, use question word order: rarely do we get.
